captionLines: The People of the State of New York, Respondent,
dateLines: Appeal, by permission of a Justice of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in the Fourth Judicial Department, from an order of that Court, entered July 26, 2024. The Appellate Division affirmed a judgment of the Onondaga County Court (Thomas J. Miller, J.), which had convicted defendant, upon a jury verdict, of murder in the second degree and criminal possession of a weapon in the second degree (four counts).

Crimes - Consolidation and Severance - Conflict Arising during Summation In the prosecution of defendant and codefendant, who were charged in a single indictment with murder and criminal possession of a weapon on an acting-in-concert theory for each firing a gun into a crowd of people while in a vehicle with a third individual, the trial court did not abuse its discretion in denying defendant's renewed request to sever his trial from that of his codefendant after codefendant's counsel argued during summation that the trial evidence supported the conclusion that defendant was one of the shooters. As neither defendant had called any witnesses or elicited incriminating evidence against the other on cross-examination, no apparent conflict in the defenses arose until summation. Where, as here, the same evidence supplies the proof against both defendants, only the most cogent reasons warrant a severance. Under the applicable two-part test, severance is required where the core of each defense is in irreconcilable conflict with the other and where there is a significant danger, as both defenses are portrayed to the trial court, that the conflict alone would lead the jury to infer defendant's guilt. Defendant raised the specter of a potential irreconcilable conflict between the defenses by initially moving to sever prior to trial, but apart from the comments made in summation, the defenses were remarkably consistent in their primary focus on discrediting the eyewitness who was in the vehicle with defendant and codefendant.

appearanceLikeLines.text: Keem Appeals, PLLC , Syracuse ( Bradley E. Keem of counsel), for appellant. I. James Everson's conviction was not supported by legally sufficient evidence. ( People v Delamota , 18 NY3d 107 ; People v Hines , 97 NY2d 56; People v Feingold , 7 NY3d 288 ; People v Heidgen , 22 NY3d 259 ; People v Ramos , 19 NY3d 133 .) II. The trial court erred in declining to sever the trial of James Everson and Amir Bordies. ( People v Morris , 27 NY3d 1096 ; People v Mahboubian , 74 NY2d 174; People v Cardwell , 78 NY2d 996; People v Wortham , 160 AD3d 431 , 37 NY3d 407; People v Osborne , 88 AD3d 1284 .)

Defendant's convictions were supported by legally sufficient evidence which showed that he shot into a group with the intent to cause the death of another person. ( People v Santi , 3 NY3d 234 ; Jackson v Virginia , 443 US 307; People v Bleakley , 69 NY2d 490; People v Hatton , 26 NY3d 364 ; People v Steinberg , 79 NY2d 673.) II. The trial court did not abuse its discretion in denying defendant's request to sever his trial from that of his codefendant because defendant failed to show that the core of each defense was in irreconcilable conflict with the other and that there was a significant danger that the conflict alone would lead the jury to infer defendant's guilt. ( People v Cardwell , 78 NY2d 996; People v Bornholdt , 33 NY2d 75; People v Baker , 14 NY3d 266 ; People v Wortham , 160 AD3d 431 , 37 NY3d 407; People v Murray , 155 AD3d 1106 .)

qualifierLines: {**44 NY3d at 490} OPINION OF THE COURT

The Appellate Division affirmed, rejecting defendant's argument that County Court abused its discretion in denying his{**44 NY3d at 492} motion to sever (229 AD3d 1349, 1350 [4th Dept 2024]). One Justice dissented, opining that severance was required under the circumstances of this case. The dissenting Justice granted defendant leave to appeal to this Court.
